Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear wave theory but often come with strong constraints and tend to dissipate due to dispersion. A recent study proposes a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models in harmonic potentials, featuring binary dark solitons which can exhibit stable self-accelerating motion. Investigations into these models reveal that self-accelerating modes are characterized by a specific relationship between the masses of the components and the chemical potentials, occurring when a specific resonance is reached. This phenomenon is further studied in the context of atomic condensates by analyzing experimental parameters and the scope of this study is also considered in terms of its implications for optical lattices.

a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms.

In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using rounded averages, specifically when U equals the average of Y divided by n. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-monetary setting: Round-Robin, Proportional, and Random (RRPR) mechanisms, as well as the Characteristic Function (CF) mechanism. We established that RRPR mechanisms result in equilibria that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, whereas CF mechanisms result in equilibria that are fair up to any good for any number of agents. Consequently, these mechanisms provide the best possible general-purpose fair allocation methods.

Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings.

high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that arise from the merger of compact binary stars or the collapse of massive stars, which can also generate gravitational waves. amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a compact LSTM structure called CompactMemory-LSTM (CML) is developed, which significantly reduces model size while maintaining accuracy. In addition to this algorithmic advancement, a hardware platform called Highly Flexible Deep Neural Network Accelerator (HF-DNA) is designed to efficiently support various deep neural network architectures, including LSTMs. Experimental results indicate that CML can yield substantial improvements in model size, a factor of up to 5 times smaller than traditional LSTMs, without sacrificing accuracy. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum linear spectroscopy that might also extend to other fields of research.

Our proposed method does not require upscaling techniques, despite modeling millions of fractures. To accommodate infinite fracture conductivity, we employ a two-step approach, first solving a singular problem and then adding a fracture-induced pressure drop. Our scheme maintains consistency with the original Darcy problem, enabling simple implementation via existing flow solvers with minimal additional cost. We leverage the MIPEC finite element library to demonstrate our method's performance on three real-world scenarios, showcasing substantial efficiency gains of our scheme compared to traditional techniques. cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online.

plets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and air flow, studying the results in still air and during gentle gusts. Our research reveals that even in calm conditions, air flow within droplets can hinder their downward journey, ultimately deciding whether the droplet settles on a surface or continues airborne. Evaporation's effect on droplet size also plays a key role in how it interacts with its surroundings, where the droplet's shape and size determine its ability to settle or become airborne. When exposed to gentle gusts of air, the behavior of evaporating droplets becomes even more complex, where changes in droplet size can shift from settling to becoming airborne, and vice versa, influenced by wind speed, droplet size, and surface tension. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to tracking the infection's spread, where clean and contaminated droplets exhibit distinct trajectories, ultimately affecting how COVID19 is spread.

Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing a comprehensive array of uncertainty quantification methods is presented, covering not only Bayesian approaches but also non Bayesian methodologies such as deep neural network ensembles, dropout, and probability concentration inequalities. The proposed framework is applied to solve a variety of problems including defocusing cubic nonlinear Schrodinger equations, the Helmholtz equation and the linear and nonlinear elasticity equations. Numerical results are presented to illustrate how different uncertainty quantification methods compare to each other.

Using a newly developed general technique and proving a newly formulated conjecture simultaneously, we have achieved significant breakthroughs in our research and have successfully answered many open questions in this field. These achievements include our successful attempts to decompose the squares of linear polynomials into the sum of squares of other polynomials and our successful attempts to find the minimum value of certain expressions that involve squares of polynomials. These successes have given us a deeper understanding of some specific instances that involve the decomposition of the squares of linear polynomials into the sum of squares of other polynomials and the minimization of expressions that involve squares of polynomials, specifically those that don't equal zero. These specific instances were first introduced by F. Kuhn in 1968 and have since been the subject of much debate.

We reevaluate how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about its unitarity. We establish two fundamental sets of experimental limitations - direct plus inherent constraints, and indirect ones. We examine the effects of each set on the possible deviation of neutrino behavior from expected unitarity. We also provide a clearer understanding of predictions related to flux and cross-sections, taking into consideration any contamination from new physics affecting hadronic measurements. We focus on the currently operating FASER$\nu$ experiment to show that certain neutrino experiments have sensitivity to this issue. We discovered that certain constraints can limit deviation from expected neutrino behavior to below $10^{-3}$, exceeding current limits on a similar problem related to other subatomic particles. However, if we consider only certain other constraints, large unitarity violations can occur and be confirmed or disproven with the currently operating FASER$\nu$ experiment in a significant margin of error.

In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic physics of quasi-S SHOWS states generated by interacting acoustic phonons. These interactions give rise to a tri-critical point and the merging of Weyl points into a cubic singularity, as well as the formation of a mid-gap state in the quasi-S SHOWS state. These features can be modulated through light quantum uses, offering a new 3D Weyl semimetal system for studying its exotic physics.

Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when trying to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in training powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments on both single-task and multi-task learning scenarios. The results showed that FedSA successfully combined knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Moreover, FedSA consistently maintained the same level of performance when compared to a non-selective approach on various subtasks. The source code and models used in this research are publicly available on the GitHub repository.

Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as a spatial metric. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations.

rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

Investigating this boundary within systems that evolve over time requires analyzing the entanglement entropy's change as a function of time. Research has shown that the change in entanglement entropy along a null direction, within systems that evolve over time, cannot be used to measure the work done on the system. However, there is evidence that the change in renormalized free energy along a null direction can be used to measure the work done on the system. In addition, studies have demonstrated that the change in renormalized free energy along a null direction can also be used to measure the change in local temperature. This research further finds that the change in renormalized free energy along a null direction can be used to measure the change in local chemical potential. In addition, we propose that the change in renormalized free energy along a null direction can be used to measure the change in local field strength. In order to measure the work done on the system, it is necessary that the change in renormalized free energy along a null direction is non-negative. This condition is known as the quantum thermodynamic null energy condition. It is worth noting that there is a more general condition, the change in renormalized free energy along a null direction being proportional to the change in local temperature, which may be used to measure the work done on the system

's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future.

To address this, researchers have developed a novel method using reaction nanoscopy on charged propanediol nanodroplets. By leveraging ultrashort laser pulses, they have established the capability to monitor the droplet's average size, charge distribution, and surrounding near-field. The quantum-inspired nature of these algorithms makes them mappable to parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), which is now fueling proposals for leveraging near-term quantum devices to enhance algorithm performance. Furthermore, joint quantum-classical frameworks can exploit the strengths of TNs and PQC models. Despite this progress, a major limitation remains in scaling TN algorithms due to classical memory constraints when using dense matrix operations. This hurdle can be overcome by utilizing tensor core operations, which are now feasible with the recent availability of TF32 data types in TensorFlow. We demonstrate a substantial speedup in scaling TN algorithms on large systems by leveraging TF32, which provides a 5-7 factor increase in performance over single precision for key matrix multiplication operations. This improvement is primarily attributed to the increased data bandwidth enabled by TF32, which is a key performance optimizer technique. We also explore strategies to achieve similar performance gains through alternative approaches, which can be applied to other tensor network algorithms.

Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon existing cell-graphs that encode cell characteristics and spatial relationships, researchers have been using machine learning to establish correlations between tissue structure and function. However, a single cell-centric approach falls short of describing the complex hierarchical organization within tissues. In response, a novel multi-scale graph representation of tissues has been proposed, comprising of multiple layers of histological entities, along with their relationships. A corresponding neural network is also proposed, along with a optimization challenge for HACT graphs in the context of breast cancer diagnosis.

A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, which is a challenge because the likelihood normalizing constant is hard to determine directly. To overcome this difficulty, we employed a class of rough normalizing constants that allow for a exploitable bound, thereby making the posterior inference feasible via MCMC methods. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach with simulated and real-world data, particularly on relationships between people in online forums as expressed through tweets.

Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that allows a model to segment similar structures in a target domain with only a limited number of target domain annotations, aided by existing annotations in a source domain. We employ Domain-Specific Batch Normalization to normalize anatomical feature maps from the two domains separately, introduce a cross-domain contrastive learning approach to promote extracting domain-invariant features, and integrate these into a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher (SE-MT) framework that leverages unlabeled target domain images and incorporates prediction consistency constraints. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the CS-CADA's ability to solve the complex cross-anatomy domain shift issue, resulting in the accurate segmentation of coronary arteries in X-ray images, aided by retinal vessel images, and cardiac MR images, aided by fundus images, with only a limited number of target domain annotations.

A straightforward examination indicates that this 1.5 order formalism is inherently defective in all contexts. Although it appears that the associated algebra is closed, a detailed examination in a simplified setting reveals the presence of a non-nilpotent BRS operator generated by the 1.5 order formalism. limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while maintaining its high energy, which has been demonstrated numerically with large amplitude circularly polarized pulses. It can effectively prevent the emergence of a second pulse with opposite polarization, even when present, according to simulations. Additionally, this waveplate can compensate for birefringence-induced pulse polarization modification in long-distance fiber optics, as shown. This type of plasma waveplate offers promising applications in the intensification of high-power laser pulses.

Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a maximum a posteriori estimator or even a machine learning approach, the neural network, that was previously shown to have superior lensing reconstruction performance when compared to the quadratic estimator in certain scenarios. We take this further by investigating these methods' performance when removing a significant amount of noise to simulate a primordial signal. We discover that the neural network estimator's delensing performance is on par with the iterative estimator, the benchmark in our field. We found that in order for these methods to work properly it is necessary to train the model under controlled conditions. MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds.

SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases.

in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is designed such that the rotation angle of the LE segments can be adjusted based on the specific astrophysical source, allowing for optimal performance and minimal requirements for data correction.

deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, models trained on density information alone failed to predict halo masses accurately, demonstrating the importance of velocity field effects on the halo collapse, particularly in certain mass scales.

This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation in favor of a first principles model comprising first-order differential equations, solving these to generate configurations that meet both hydrostatic equilibrium and rotational balance requirements. This algorithm relies on a precise method for solving the balance equations, TDFSS, which was particularly optimized for this application, yielding results that demonstrate a level of precision equivalent to 10^-8 in the balance equations. Our technique involves a range of 1000 to 10000 grid points across the star's circumference, yielding results that accurately mirror exact solutions at a level of 10^-5 in terms of mass fraction. This method's construction ensures that configurations obtained through it possess the desired characteristics of rotational equilibrium, which is validated by observing that the angular momentum remains constant across all fluid elements. This method is suitable for applying forces like gravitational waves, which act on a specific interval of the star, and it provides an alternative to the conventional method for solving the Euler equation.

Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. avitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy.

However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. This study aims to investigate changes in urban diversity, including both physical and social aspects, which occurred as a result of these restrictions. Methodologically, we used geographic information systems and social network analysis to compare pre- and during-pandemic periods, which revealed a notable decrease in diversity across all measured factors. Specifically, we observed reduced foot traffic in urban areas by 50% and a decline in visits to cultural institutions by 70%, which led to decreased professional and social interactions among city dwellers. Consequently, we urge policymakers to implement digital technologies that facilitate online interactions and promote diverse urban experiences, which are also essential for promoting physical activity among older adults.

Yet, little attention has been given to assessing 5G cellular tower exposure among children and occupants of sensitive locations, including schools and medical facilities. To address these concerns, a systematic approach is outlined to numerically evaluate downlink 5G exposure among children, adolescents, schools, and medical centers, also applicable to pre-5G scenarios. , has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently compiled to use the SIMD instructions found in modern processors.  To facilitate easy adoption, we created a high-level SMMO language called RapidObject (RO).  RO features intuitive vectorized object operations and a compact, efficient code format that can directly utilize GPU SIMD instructions.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of RO, we developed a set of high-performance applications across science, engineering, and finance fields by modifying existing C codes.  When running these applications on a high-end GPU, we observed significant speed gains, with some achieving 10 to 30 times faster performance and one application seeing a staggering 180 times improvement in performance.  This paper delves into the design of the RO compiler, showcases the performance gains achieved with RO, and compares its results to other parallel programming approaches.

X-ray emission line mapping, essential for studying ICM turbulence, is complicated by the lack of high-resolution spectroscopy. Future X-ray detectors like the X-IFU on Athena will enable thorough investigations of ICM turbulence across multiple scales. Crucial metrics for such studies include line shift and broadening maps, as well as the second-order structure function. When analyzing these quantities, measurements are constrained by instrumental uncertainties and the inherent variability in cosmic observations. Here, the formalism established in a previous paper is expanded to account for the statistical uncertainty in line diagnostics, specifically structure functions. Statistical variance contributes to total variance in several ways, influenced by the detector's geometry, spatial binning, and the characteristics of turbulent fields. These terms hold significant importance for studying turbulence at smaller scales. A demonstration is conducted for the X-IFU using a simulated turbulent velocity map of a galaxy cluster resembling Coma. Results indicate excellent agreement with theoretical formulas for structure function estimation and its associated variance. These derived expressions can be applied to any X-ray measurement of turbulent structure functions and provide a framework for optimizing future instrumentation and observational strategies.

Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have identified rough limits to the ratio of the toroidal and poloidal magnetic energy. In order to define the conditions necessary for these stable configurations, we ran three-dimensional simulations utilizing the Pencil Code for non-rotating stars experiencing viscosity-driven dissipation. Our simulations were performed for both barotropic stars with constant specific entropy and stably stratified stars, while varying parameters including the level of stable stratification and magnetic energy in each component, confirming existing predictions for the stability boundaries.

Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the long-held'mass problem' hypothesis, which suggests that massive stars form through the merger of low-mass protostars.  Instead, it provides evidence for a mass-growth model in which massive stars can directly develop from massive, quiescent star-forming cores, with the Drirc locus providing a notable example.

The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The formation of the cyclical compounds in TMC-1 can be attributed to a reaction pathway based on neutral-neutral reactions, which also suggests benzene's expected abundance should be comparable to that of cyclopentadiene.

Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending this process. In the early 2000s, grid computing represented the future of computer science. Some interpreted it as a way to provide seamless access to diverse resources. Others saw it as a means to achieve peer-to-peer coordination on a large scale. From a translational perspective, we believe grid computing was about providing a standard framework that allowed researchers to develop applications on top of it, regardless of the underlying infrastructure. This perspective guides our analysis of the life cycle of grid computing in Australia. We discuss the accomplishments and challenges faced during the project's various stages. These include the initial project planning, the development of the Australian Access Grid, the establishment of the Australian Grid, the creation of the Australian Grid e-Science, and the integration of grid computing with cloud and data-intensive research.

This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. AR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance.

Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the pyroptotic process by disrupting the NLRP3 inflammasome, thus delaying the release of IL-1β and IL-18.  Our model demonstrates that targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome through these medications leads to an increased risk of bacterial translocation, which can result in the release of lipopolysaccharides, or the overflow of these toxins, leading to sepsis.  Our analysis also suggests that delaying the release of IL-1β and IL-18 through NLRP3 inflammasome disruption may trigger a cytokine storm, characterized by the rapid release of these cytokines, leading to the host's death.  In contrast, the gradual release of these cytokines may facilitate the host's immune system in eliminating the virus, as seen with mild COVID-19 cases.  Our mathematical model highlights the importance of managing pyroptosis to prevent the cytokine storm that contributes to the high mortality rates observed in severe COVID-19 cases.

Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement.

Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed in this paper that dynamically optimizes training levels across individual single-hop links, maximizing overall spectral efficiency. To tackle this optimization problem in the presence of noise, a realistic THz channel model, and limited processing capacity, the proposed algorithm leverages opinion division and dynamic updating of locally optimal solutions. Simulations show the proposed technique can reduce beam training time while maintaining similar performance with respect to coherent training, and can handle a higher number of nodes compared to exhaustive search.

Focusing on temperate worlds surrounded by thick H2 atmospheres, our models follow chemical transformations and gas circulation after H2O, CH4, NH3, and H2S molecules break apart under stellar radiation, utilizing K2-18 b, PH2 b, and Kepler-167 e as prime examples. According to our simulations, NH3 molecules are destroyed by solar radiation in atmospheres surrounding G/K stars, while intact in those surrounding M stars. Typically, NH3 breaks down in presence of CH4, producing GH3+ and e- particles that trigger atmospheric electron jets. These jets, in turn, split water molecules, producing H and OH ions which then react with CH4, NH3, and H2O to form respective molecules. As a result of this process, water molecules are constantly re-mixed with other species across the planet's day-night boundary, resulting in strong winds that could shape the clouds and hazes often observed in these exoplanets. Furthermore, presence of electron jets might explain the diverse spectral features, accounting for the absorption and reflection of starlight, as well as possible bi-directional stellar light polarization detected in some exoplanets.

Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various representations. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion.

we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and it flexibly handles complex geometry obstacles and source and observation points. A direct issue with traditional approaches is the complex construction of the acoustic scattering operator, but our simple single-source simulation framework bypasses this difficulty. Instead, we leverage a limited number of simple reference configurations to obtain a set of reduced-order modes, which are then specific solutions to the scattering problem. These modes are organized into an empirical interpolation matrix, through which we can combine them to handle broader application scenarios. This process is based on empirical observations and doesn't draw from analytical data. Ultimately, a discrete empirical system is established from which we can synthesize the empirical interpolation matrix. Once this matrix is determined, we can efficiently handle the complex construction of the acoustic scattering operator via a simple and fast adaptive process. This adaptive procedure systematically refines a subset of the reference modes until they provide sufficient accuracy for a given target frequency. It leverages the optimality of the single-source simulation framework and the efficiency of the empirical interpolation method, resulting in computational costs that are essentially independent of the frequency parameter.

In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process.

By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models.

These elements equate to preimages under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism of induced matrix coefficients of special idempotents in the group algebra Z[e_(n)]Sym(n). In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada.

For domains with smooth boundaries, a straightforward and efficient method involves dividing the boundary into smaller segments to approximate the potential using complex linear combinations, specifically conforming to Hermite interpolatory polynomials.
